function.name: cronjob
function.description:
Manage scheduled cron jobs with a single compressed tool.

Use action='create' to schedule a new job from a prompt or one or more skills.
Use action='list' to inspect jobs.
Use action='update', 'pause', 'resume', 'remove', or 'run' to manage an existing job.

To stop a job the user no longer wants: first action='list' to find the job_id, then action='remove' with that job_id. Never guess job IDs — always list first.

Jobs run in a fresh session with no current-chat context, so prompts must be self-contained.
If skills are provided on create, the future cron run loads those skills in order, then follows the prompt as the task instruction.
On update, passing skills=[] clears attached skills.

NOTE: The agent's final response is auto-delivered to the target. Put the primary
user-facing content in the final response. Cron jobs run autonomously with no user
present — they cannot ask questions or request clarification.

Important safety rule: cron-run sessions should not recursively schedule more cron jobs.

action.description: One of: create, list, update, pause, resume, remove, run

prompt.description: For create: the full self-contained prompt. If skills are also provided, this becomes the task instruction paired with those skills.

repeat.description: Optional repeat count. Omit for defaults (once for one-shot, forever for recurring).

deliver.description: Omit this parameter to auto-deliver back to the current chat and topic (recommended). Auto-detection preserves thread/topic context. Only set explicitly when the user asks to deliver somewhere OTHER than the current conversation. Values: 'origin' (same as omitting), 'local' (no delivery, save only), or platform:chat_id:thread_id for a specific destination. Examples: 'telegram:-1001234567890:17585', 'discord:#engineering', 'sms:+15551234567'. WARNING: 'platform:chat_id' without :thread_id loses topic targeting.

skills.description: Optional ordered list of skill names to load before executing the cron prompt. On update, pass an empty array to clear attached skills.

model.description: Optional per-job model override. If provider is omitted, the current main provider is pinned at creation time so the job stays stable.

provider.description: Provider name (e.g. 'openrouter', 'anthropic'). Omit to use and pin the current provider.

script.description: Optional path to a Python script that runs before each cron job execution. Its stdout is injected into the prompt as context. Use for data collection and change detection. Relative paths resolve under ~/.hermes/scripts/. On update, pass empty string to clear.

context_from.description: Optional job ID or list of job IDs whose most recent completed output is injected into the prompt as context before each run. Use this to chain cron jobs: job A collects data, job B processes it. Each entry must be a valid job ID (from cronjob action='list'). Note: injects the most recent completed output — does not wait for upstream jobs running in the same tick. On update, pass an empty array to clear.

enabled_toolsets.description: Optional list of toolset names to restrict the job's agent to (e.g. ["web", "terminal", "file", "delegation"]). When set, only tools from these toolsets are loaded, significantly reducing input token overhead. When omitted, all default tools are loaded. Infer from the job's prompt — e.g. use "web" if it calls web_search, "terminal" if it runs scripts, "file" if it reads files, "delegation" if it calls delegate_task. On update, pass an empty array to clear.

workdir.description: Optional absolute path to run the job from. When set, AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / .cursorrules from that directory are injected into the system prompt, and the terminal/file/code_exec tools use it as their working directory — useful for running a job inside a specific project repo. Must be an absolute path that exists. When unset (default), preserves the original behaviour: no project context files, tools use the scheduler's cwd. On update, pass an empty string to clear. Jobs with workdir run sequentially (not parallel) to keep per-job directories isolated.

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

{"content": "   166|## Chapter 4: The Garage
   167|
   168|*Where wood, oil, and patience built more than models*
   169|
   170|You know how some places just feel different the moment you walk in? Like the air itself has a different weight? That's how the garage felt.  If the dinner table was where my father's Navy training went to die—rigid, oppressive, all about obedience—the garage was where he became someone else entirely. Someone Bob actually wanted to be around.
   171|
   172|Bob was ten. Maybe eleven. He doesn’t remember exactly, but he remembers the smell. God, that smell. Glue, sharp and sweet—that distinctive petroleum tang that clung to your sent. Balsa bits everywhere, Silence that wasn't awkward, just... companionable.  This was the smell of possibility. Of things being built instead of broken. Of knowledge passing from one pair of hands to another without a single order being given.
   173|
   174|Bobs father let him use a scroll saw one afternoon. Heavy thing, cast iron, probably made by back in the '40s.—and the tool felt awkward, dangerous even. "Show you something," he said. Not "Do this." Not "Pay attention." Just... show you something. He took a board—pine, maybe a foot long, —and demonstrated. One careful cut, shaving off a ribbon of wood so thin you could almost see through it.  "Your turn." Bob, then Bobby, flinched, waiting for the yell, the criticism, the "for Christ's sake, Bobby" that I knew so well from dinner. He adjusted Bobby’s grip. Moved the left hand forward. Shifted "Feel it," he said. And here's the thing—his voice was different in the garage. Softer. Like he was talking to the wood as much as to me. "The saw blade will tell you what it wants if you listen."  That was a different language. Not the Navy language of commands and compliance. This was... I don't know. Something older. The wood had grain, see, and if you went against it, you'd feel the resistance before the tool even bit. You'd hear it in the change of sound, feel it in your hands through the plane's body. Competence mattered more than compliance here. Understanding trumped obedience. Bob didn't know those words then. The garage had its own rules, its own hierarchy, and it operated on a currency Bob was starting to understand. Skill. Not rank. Not volume. Not how loud you could yell. Just... could you make the thing work? Could you make it well.
   175|
   176|### The Boat
   177|
   178|The project that would eat up a year of Bobs lives sat in the middle of that garage like a promise. Sixteen feet of wooden boat and a trailer built from plans had ordered from some magazine—it  was Popular Mechanics, not certain. Could have been Mechanix Illustrated. They both had those glossy covers with guys in work shirts holding tools. It was ambitious. Probably too ambitious for a boy in school. But that was part of what made it matter.
   179|
   180|The boat wasn't practical. Let me be honest—we had no lake house. No realistic plan for where this sixteen-foot vessel would actually live once we finished it. My mother pointed this out exactly once, standing in the kitchen doorway with her arms crossed, watching Bob and his brother carry the first frames through to the garage for cutting. "Where exactly is this going?" she asked. "We'll figure that out.". And that was that. Practicality wasn't the point. Bob understands that now, in a way he couldn’t then. The point was the building. The frame went up first it looked impossibly fragile standing on its own until the ribs went in. They curved like whale bones—there's a cliché for you, but I'm telling you, that's what they looked like. Giving the structure shape and strength. He learned to steam-bend wood. You wrap wood in wet rags—heavy cotton rags—and heat them over a washtub of boiling water until they became pliable. Then you bend them around forms before they cool and set into new curves. The physics of it fascinated me, though I didn't have the words for it then. How heat could temporarily defeat the structural memory of cellulose. How water acted as a plasticizer. How the wood would hold its new shape once dry, like it had forgotten it was ever straight. Bob, and his father, and eventually his Son, was an intuitive engineer. A men who understood forces and stresses through feel and experience. He could look at a structure and know if it was sound, could sense when a joint was weak or a line was true, without being able to articulate exactly why.   Even then, Bob wanted to know why. He pored over those plans, studying the drawings, trying to understand the principles behind the design. Why did the ribs need to be where they were? What was the purpose of the keelson versus the keel? How did the planking work, each board overlapping the one below like shingles on a roof, creating a hull that was both strong and flexible? The questions sometimes annoyed him. He pr... [truncated]
   181|
   182|### The Lessons of Mistakes
   183|
   184|We made errors. Of course we did. I wish I could tell you some inspiring story about how we were naturals, how everything was perfect. But that's not how it happened.
   185|
   186|When things didn’t Bob was devastated. Actually devastated. He was thirteen, maybe fourteen, old enough to understand what mistakes had cost us. There was wisdom in that I wouldn't fully appreciate until decades later, when I was managing engineering teams and teaching my own children. The philosophy of the garage—iterative improvement, learning from failure, the value of craftsmanship over speed—became foundational to how I approached problems throughout my life. But at the time, it was simply how things were done. You measured twice and cut once not because someone had invented that saying, but because wasting a twelve-dollar piece of plywood mattered when you were a child working on lemonade sales. You sanded by hand because you father didn’t have a power sander. 
   187|
   188|Something else, something Bob is not proud of. There were days he didn't want to be there. Days when his friends were playing baseball or riding bikes or doing whatever normal thirteen-year-olds did, and I was in that garage.
   189|
   190|I resented it. God help me, I resented it. That was its own kind of lesson. The universe doesn't negotiate. Materials don't care about your feelings. You can be angry at a piece of wood all day long, but it's not going to cut itself. Now Bob  understands what he was learning . It wasn't just building . It was... . Resilience? Responsibility? The understanding that showing up matters more than feeling like it? Bob is still learning that one, honestly.
   191|
   192|### His Mother's Wisdom 
   193|
   194|The garage was only half the story. Maybe less than half. While Bob’s father taught Bob to build, his mother taught him to think with care. To plan before acting. To see the world as a series of interconnected systems where preparation mattered as much as execution. "Measure twice, cut once," she would say, watching from the kitchen doorway as Bob and his father and I carried Model kits through to the garage. She'd picked up the phrase during the Depression, and she applied it to everything. Not just woodworking. Decisions. Relationships. The architecture of a life well-lived. The phrase became a touchstone for me. A reminder that impulsiveness carried costs that preparation could avoid. Bobs mother embodied this philosophy in every aspect of her domestic engineering. She planned meals in advance, shopped with lists, kept a budget written in her neat accountant's hand. Where my father operated on intuition and experience, she operated on systems and forethought.
   195|
   196|One afternoon—I must have been fourteen, maybe fifteen—she caught me in the quiet aftermath of one of those dinner table confrontations that left me angry and humiliated. I was in the living room, I think, pretending to read a book but actually just staring at the same page, boiling with that particular teenage rage that has no outlet. She sat down next to me. Didn't say anything for a minute. Just sat there, her hand on my knee, warm and solid. "Your father is a good man," she said finally. "But he doesn't know how to be soft. The war made him hard, and his own father made him harder." Bob wanted to argue. Wanted to tell her she was wrong, that he wasn't a good man, that good men didn't yell at their sons "He's afraid, Robert," she said. And she used my real name, not the casual "Rob" everyone else used by that time. "Afraid he won't raise you right. Afraid you'll make the mistakes he made. The yelling is fear wearing anger's clothes." This was her gift to Bob. Translation. She helped me understand the man who seemed impossible to understand, decoding the emotional language of a generation that had learned to suppress vulnerability. She taught me that love could be buried beneath harshness, that discipline could coexist with devotion, that the father who demanded so much did so because he cared too much rather than too little. Bob didn't fully believe her then. How could I? I was fifteen, and fifteen-year-olds know everything, which is to say they know nothing. But the seed was planted. And years later, when Bob was old enough to look back with some distance, he realized she'd been right Not about everything. Maybe not even about most things. But about that.
   197|
   198|She also taught Bob practical things. Critical things. If the garage was my father's domain, the kitchen was her laboratory, and she made sure I learned my way around it. Not because cooking was women's work—she rejected that notion entirely—but because independence required competence, and competence required practice.  "A man who can't feed himself is a man dependent on others," she said, teaching me to make an omelet at age twelve. "Your father never learned and look at him—lost if I'm not there to put a plate in front of him.. You're going to live alone. You need to know how to take care of yourself." She taught Bob the chemistry of cooking, though she never used that word. How heat transformed proteins. How acids balanced fats. How the Maillard reaction—she didn't call it that, just said "browning. She was not a great cook but she knew how to cook with limited ingredients, money was often tight. These lessons carried survival value. When Bob went to college, He watched classmates when they moved off-campus and discovered they couldn't cook.  More than survival, cooking taught me patience. A different patience than woodworking, but related. You couldn't rush a braise. You couldn't force bread to rise. You had to work with the ingredients, understand their properties, respect their timelines. My mother's kitchen operated on the same principles as my father's garage: understand your materials, prepare properly, execute with care. Bob thinks about her sometimes. She has been gone for years now, but she's still in that kitchen. Still teaching.
   199|
   200|### The Partnership
   201|
   202|Watching Bob’s parents together, he began to understand that their marriage was itself a kind of complex system where two very different people had found ways to complement each other. His father provided and protected, fixed what broke, handled the physical world. Has mother managed, planned, maintained the emotional infrastructure that kept the family functioning. She moderated his father. When his temper flared at the dinner table, she would intervene—not by contradicting him, which would escalate things, but by redirection. By subtle calibration. By the quiet authority she had established through years of competence. She knew when to let things go and when to step in, when to support her husband publicly and when to talk sense into him privately. "Don't judge your father by his worst moments," she told Bob once. He was sixteen, maybe seventeen, old enough to think he understood everything about disappointment. "Judge him by his consistency. By what he provides. By the fact that he never leaves, never gives up, never stops working for this family." "He doesn't know how to say he loves you. But he shows it every day." This perspective—seeing the whole system rather than isolated failures—became essential to Bobs own development as a parent and partner. He learned from her that relationships required translation, that different people expressed care in different languages, that the task of family was to build bridges across those differences rather than demanding uniformity.
   203|
   204|She also taught Bob resilience, though she would never have used that word. When money was tight, she made it stretch. When his father was difficult, she found ways to manage. When he struggled with school or friendships or the thousand challenges of growing up, she listened without judgment, offered perspective without taking over, believed in my capacity to solve my own problems while remaining ready to help. "I don't want you to be like your father," she said once, surprising Bob. They were in the kitchen, folding laundry together—this must have been his junior year of high school—and he said something about how he would never yell at my kids the way he yelled at me. "I want you to be like yourself. Take his good parts—his work ethic, his loyalty, his ability to make things. Leave behind the parts that hurt. That's how generations get better. Not by copying, but by selecting." This was evolution, she explained. Cultural evolution, family evolution, the slow process by which each generation could improve on the last by keeping what worked and discarding what didn't. It required awareness, which my father sometimes lacked, and intention, which she possessed in abundance.  Bob thinks about that conversation a lot now. About selection. About what he kept from my parents and what he discarded. He kept the work ethic. Kept the belief that showing up matters. Kept the understanding that love is a verb, not a feeling. He discarded the yelling. The rigidity. The belief that obedience was more important than understanding. His mother would be proud of that, he thinks. Or maybe she'd just nod and say "Good. Now help me fold these sheets."
   205|
   206|### The Engineering of Everything
   207|
   208|The building wasn't the only education happening in the garage. My father had an old electronics, not that you would call them that now,—tube-type, pre-transistor, probably from the late '40s—and Bob learned how they worked. The process seemed almost mystical. Invisible signals pulled from the air, transformed by glowing filaments and magnetic coils, emerging as voices and music from a paper cone. How was that even possible? How could sound travel through nothing? "Electricity is just organized lightning," his father explained one afternoon, showing Bob how to read the resistor color codes. Black, brown, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, gray, white. Zero through nine. He memorized that sequence without really understanding why, the way you memorize the alphabet before you understand what reading is for. His brothers never understood the secrets of electricity they never seemed interested. His father showed him how to solder without cold joints. How to trace a circuit from power supply to output. How to use a multimeter, the needle dancing across the scale as you found the right range. "It wants to get from here to there," His father said, pointing at the schematic. "Your job is to give it a path and control how much gets through." Bob started building his own projects. A crystal radio that needed no batteries, pulling its power from the radio waves themselves—a little wooden box with a coil of wire and a crystal detector, and if you put the headphones on just right and tuned the coil with the little slider, you could pull in the strongest local station. Detroit, usually. Clear as a bell on a good night. A simple amplifier constructed from plans in a library book. An electric motor built from wire, magnets, and a battery, spinning proof of Faraday's laws made visible. Each success led to greater ambition. Each failure led to deeper understanding. The garage became my laboratory, my sanctuary, the place where the theoretical knowledge I absorbed from books me... [truncated]
   209|
   210|My father watched this evolution with something like pride, though he would never have used that word. "You've got good hands," he said once, which was high praise indeed. In the garage, curiosity was not just tolerated but valued. Understanding the why was as important as achieving the result. This was engineering in its purest form: the marriage of theoretical knowledge and practical skill, the art of making ideas real. Bob didn't know it then, but he was building something more important than radios or motors or model aircraft. I was building a way of being in the world. A framework for understanding. The confidence that came from knowing I could figure things out, could take something broken and make it whole, could start with nothing but raw materials and end with something that worked. That confidence would carry Bob through engineering school. Through early career setbacks. Through the inevitable crises of adult life. It had been built here, plank by plank, wire by wire, mistake by mistake.
   211|
   212|### The Father Beneath the Uniform
   213|
   214|Working alongside my father in the garage, Bob began to see the man beneath the Navy veteran. Beneath the authoritarian parent. Beneath the provider who carried the weight of a family's survival on his shoulders. Bob learned other things too. How his father wanted to be an architect, but the war had derailed those plans. How he'd met my mother—really met her, not just the bare facts of their elopement—during a chance encounter.. How he'd known within minutes that she was the one. How terrified he'd been at becoming a father. Certain he would repeat the mistakes of his own harsh upbringing his father being a womanizer and gambler when on the road as a train engineer. "I swore I'd be different," he said one evening, fitting a breasthook into the bow while I held it steady. The breasthook was this curved piece of wood that reinforced the joint where the bow timbers met, and it had to be perfect or the whole front of the boat would be weak. "Then you were born and I had no idea what I was doing. So I fell back on what I knew. The Navy way." He didn't apologize. That wasn't his way. But the admission hung in the air between them, an acknowledgment of damage done, a recognition that the man in the house and the man in the garage were not quite the same person, and that the former had sometimes failed the son he truly loved. I didn't know what to say. Bob was seventeen by then, old enough to understand complexity but young enough to still want simple answers. That is when when Bob understood something: sometimes love isn't about the words. Sometimes it's about showing up. About teaching someone to build. About trusting them with expensive tools and dangerous equipment and the space to make mistakes. He never said "I love you" much. But he was there. Every Saturday. For years. Teaching Bob what he knew. Letting Bob become someone he couldn't be.
   215|
   216|### Independence
   217|
   218|By the time Bob was fourteen, he had outgrown the role of assistant. More significantly, he had acquired his own projects. 
   219|
   220|### The Boat Floats
   221|
   222|Bob and his brother launched it on a cool spring morning. The boat wasn't perfect—it showed variations Bobs skills had evolved during the build, It moved through the lake with a grace that seemed impossible for something built by amateurs in a suburban garage. My brother rowed first, testing the trim, checking for leaks. Then we put up the sail, and Bob settled onto the rear seat and felt the boat respond to my body, becoming an extension of my intentions. It creaked. Water lapped against the hull. And Bob understood, truly understood for the first time, what creation felt like. It didn’t last long soon the center board, made from cheap plywood broke and Bob and his brother were towed back to shore, but it was enough-it sailed. We never used the boat much after that. It sat in the garage,, then in a storage shed, then—later—was sold to someone else who probably never knew the history in its imperfect seams. The point had never been the boat itself. The point was the building. When Bob looks back on that spring morning, what he remembers most was my brother’s face. The eyes were bright with an emotion that I would later recognize as love. Not the demanding love of expectation, but the generous love of seeing someone you care about.
   223|
   224|### The Garage Stays Open
   225|
   226|High school brought new interests. New demands. New distractions. I still spent time in the garage, but less of it. There were girls now, and a part-time job at the local TV repair shop, and the looming decisions about college and career that would carry me away from that place and into my own life.  But the foundation had been laid. In the garage, I'd learned that I was capable of building complex things from raw materials. I'd learned that knowledge could be acquired through persistence, that skill came from repetition, that mistakes were tuition paid toward mastery. I'd learned that my father contained multitudes—not just the authoritarian figure who dominated my childhood, but a craftsman, a teacher, a man who had his own disappointments and dreams and who had tried, in his imperfect way, to give his son the tools for a better life. Years later when Bob brought his own children to the Garage his father no longer had the patience to tutor children from the beginning. The grandchildren never saw the best in Bobs father, that made Bob sad.
   227|
   228|Years later, when I had my own children, I tried to recreate this magic. I built a workbench in my own garage. Bought tools and lumber and plans. Invited my son to build things together, to learn through doing, to discover the satisfaction of creation. It wasn't the same, of course. My son and daughter had different interests. Different talents. Different paths they wanted to walk. But the principle held. The time together mattered. The transmission of knowledge, of confidence, of the specific joy that comes from making something real with your own hands—that still worked, even across the changed landscape of a different generation.
   229|
   230|Bob sometimes wonders what his father felt, whether he knew, in some wordless way, that we were building more than toy airplanes. Whether he understood that the real project was the son standing beside him, learning to trust his own competence, preparing to row out into waters his father would never navigate. The garage door still opened on those evenings, spilling light into the suburban dark, the smell of sawdust and oil drifting out like incense. Inside, two people bent to their work, passing time together in the shared language of making, building something that would outlast them both. The belief that transformation was possible. That raw materials could become beautiful. That the right combination of knowledge and effort could create things that that mattered.
   231|
   232|**Transition: From Wood to Stars**
   233|
   234|The skills learned in that garage—the patience to measure twice, the courage to fail and rebuild, the understanding that invisible forces could be harnessed to do extraordinary things—would soon find an outlet far beyond anything Bob could have imagined. The Space Race had begun, and a boy who had learned to models and troubleshoot radios was about to discover that his hands could help build something that would reach for the stars themselves.
   235|
   236|## Chapter 5: The Spark Ignites
   237|
   238|### The TV Repair Shop
   239|
   240|The summer before tenth grade, Bob's father announced that it was time for his son to learn what work actually meant. Not the abstract work of school assignments, not the project work of the garage, but the clock-punching, customer-serving, money-earning work that occupied the majority of adult life. He had arranged a job for Bob at Hendricks TV & Electronics, a small repair shop that smelled of solder flux and ozone and the particular mustiness of vacuum tubes past their prime.  Mr. Hendricks was a bald man with perpetually cigarette -stained fingers and a habit of talking to himself while he worked. He took one look at the fifteen-year-old standing in his doorway and said, "Can you solder?"-"Yes, sir."-"Show me." Bob spent the next ten minutes demonstrating what he knew—how to tin an iron, how to heat the joint rather than the solder, how to create that bright, concave fillet that meant a good connection. Mr. Hendricks watched without comment, then handed him a basket of vacuum tubes. "Test these. The checker is in the back. Write down which ones are bad. When you're done, sweep the floor, your hired. After that, we'll see about teaching you something." The job paid $1.25 an hour, minimum wage, but what it offered in education was worth far more. Bob spent that summer and the two that followed driving around town doing pickup and delivery with a older worker and learning the applied electronics that would form the foundation of his career. He learned to read schematic diagrams, those intricate maps of electron flow that turned abstract symbols into working circuits. He learned to trace signals through televisions and radios, to identify failure points by symptom, to repair rather than replace because customers couldn't afford new sets.
   241|
   242|Soon after he encountered his first computer—not in the shop, but through his school . Dr. Richardson taught mathematics Bob noticed the man carried a textbook titled *Introduction to Digital Computers*. "You interested in that sort of thing?" Dr. Richardson asked, watching Bob eye the book. "I don't really know what it is, sir. I've read about them in magazines."
   243|
   244|"Come by the sometime. I'll show you our machine. It's not much—an IBM 1620 used for payroll —but it's a real computer. We program it on weekends when it is not being used. Make it do calculations, process data, solve problems. It's like having a very fast, very stupid assistant that follows instructions perfectly." Bob went the following Saturday. The computer filled a room, cabinets of transistors and magnetic core memory, spinning tape drives that sounded like sewing machines on amphetamines. Dr. Richardson showed him how to punch cards, how to write simple programs in raw assembly code, how the machine translated human instructions into the binary language of on-off switches and gates that was all the hardware understood.
   245|
   246|"This is the future” -. "Everything is going to change. Transportation, communication, manufacturing. You want to be part of that change; you need to understand these machines." That afternoon, Bob decided he would be an electrical engineer. Not a decision made in isolation. He wanted to work with these machines, these thinking engines that were transforming the world. He wanted to understand capabilities that had not been imagined yet. Yet the room sized computer of that time had a ten thousand time less compute than a modern mobile phone.
   247|
   248|### The First Car
   249|
   250|Bobs first car was a Chrysler valiant. It was blue, and had a mind of its own.     24|
    25|We made errors. I wish I could tell you some inspiring story about how we were naturals, how everything was perfect. But that's not how it happened.

    40|
    41|### The Partnership
    42|
    43|Watching my parents together, I began to see their marriage as a kind of complex system where two very different people complemented each other.     45|This perspective—seeing the whole system rather than isolated failures—became essential to my own development as a parent and partner. Relationships required translation.     46|
